title: why they're called words, not commandments
hook: why they're called words, not commandments
carry: ten sentences to build a life on

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sinai, and the answer we will do, and we will hear. Your line was do first. Did you do one thing before you felt ready? Day thirteen.

Two stone tablets with rounded tops: on a courthouse wall, in an old movie with a parting sea, on a classroom poster. The Ten Commandments. Ten rules, carved in stone. Here's the surprise: the Torah's own Hebrew name for them is something else. And the very first of them, the way Jews count, has no "thou shalt" in it. It doesn't tell anybody to do anything. So what is it, and why is it first? Today: the ten sentences, and why they're called words.
screen: `TWO TABLETS, ROUNDED TOPS.` → `THE TORAH CALLS THEM WORDS.` → `THE FIRST ONE HAS NO THOU SHALT.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew they're aseret ha-dibrot, the ten sayings, or, as the Torah itself puts it in Exodus and Deuteronomy, the ten words. Devarim. Words, things said, things spoken to someone. Not a legal code posted on a wall. Something said, out loud, to a people standing at a mountain. And the first word, as Jews count them, is this. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." On its face, no rule. An introduction. Maimonides later read a commandment inside it, to know that God exists, but as spoken, it reads like a greeting. Before anything is asked of you, you're told who is speaking and what they've already done for you. A relationship first, then everything else. Traditions number the ten a little differently. In the Jewish count, that opening sentence is the first word, and no other gods and no idols together are the second. Christian churches divide them in their own ways: Catholics and Lutherans one way, Orthodox and Reformed churches another. Same text, different ways of dividing it. Then the tablets. An old midrash teaches they were five and five. The first tablet is between people and God: I am, no idols, the name, the Sabbath, and honor your parents, placed there because parents are partners in giving life. The second is between people: don't murder, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't lie in court, don't covet. And the midrash reads across the tablets: "thou shalt not murder" sits opposite "I am the LORD thy God," to teach that harming a person is harming the image of God. Tradition counts six hundred and thirteen commandments in the Torah, and some teachers, Saadia Gaon among them, read these ten as the headings of all of them.
screen: `DEVARIM — WORDS, NOT RULES.` · `THE FIRST WORD IS AN INTRODUCTION.` · `FIVE AND FIVE, READ ACROSS.` · `THE HEADINGS OF SIX HUNDRED THIRTEEN.` · then, large: `I AM THE LORD THY GOD.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Go through the second tablet slowly, one at a time: don't murder, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't lie about someone, don't covet. Stop on whichever one catches. For some people it's the last, the wanting. Just notice it. The bell holds the time.
The Ten Words. Not ten rules in stone but ten sayings, beginning with an introduction: I am the one who brought you out. Thirteenth word.
Your line: ten sentences to build a life on. Today, pick one of the ten and let it be the only one you think about, all day. Day thirteen.

howItsDone: Jews read the Ten Words aloud in synagogue when they come up in the yearly Torah cycle and on the festival of Shavuot, and in some congregations people stand to hear them.

original.note: Hebrew: the ten sayings. the Torah itself says aseret ha-devarim, the ten words.

trapdoor: what you thought: ten rules carved in stone.
what it means: ten sayings spoken to a people, starting not with a rule but with who is speaking.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 34:28 and Deuteronomy 4:13 call them the ten words. the Mekhilta reads the tablets across, five facing five, and some teachers read the ten as headings of the 613.
